When the WALDENSIANS <note>The Waldensians are a medieval Christian movement that faced severe persecution and eventually joined the Protestant Reformation.</note>, in the thirty-first year of this current century <note>1731</note>, were supported in their oppression by the generous charity of the Sovereigns of our Fatherland, and a General Collection was held in our Provinces for their benefit, many were eager to know these Ancient Confessors of the Faith more closely. This moved me to investigate their origins and further fates; from this was born the description of *their history until the end of the 12th Christian century.* The volume which contained this report I published in the year 1732: with the intention, if I did not lack time, inclination, and ability, to continue that history until the *Reformation*, and subsequently until our own *age*. This was the reason why I presented the published work in the form of a *First Volume*;

The weighty work of my Ministry, along with other writings and occupations, have prevented me from progressing as quickly as I had first intended. *But*, added to this was primarily what happened to me, which JOSEPHUS (*) says somewhere of himself. Thus, what I send forth here as a specimen will give the reader an idea of how the *Apostasy* <note>original: *Afval*. # PREFACE.

...to be able to serve; I shall remember them with respect regarding that in this little work of mine.

One will soon discover how I proceeded in the preparation of these pages. Everything I found anywhere, I weighed individually, compared it with other accounts, rejected all that was too uncertain, and retained that which seemed to me to have signs of probability. The writings I mainly made use of are those of **Mornay**, **Illyricus**, **Spanheim**, **Mellinus**, **Leger**, **Du Pin**, **Fleury**, **Bossuet**, **Basnage**, and **Pictet**; besides a multitude of others, the list of which follows hereafter. I have not been able to obtain the writings of **Rainerus**, **Alanus** (*), and other old Roman <note>original: "Roomsche," meaning Roman Catholic writers</note> writers against and concerning the **Waldensians**; however, that deficiency has been compensated for by the concise extracts found in the *Library of Ecclesiastical Authors* <note>original: "Bibliotheque des Auteurs Ecclesiastiques"</note> by **Du Pin**: on which I could rely all the more because I could rest assured that he, as a Roman Catholic, would not hide what was most advantageous for his party.

Furthermore, I do not need to plead much for the necessity of my undertaking. There are some reports of the **Waldensians** in our Netherlands: but what kind they are, he who compares them with others will best determine. That of Mr. **Leger**, in his lifetime a Minister among these Believers, is indeed the best; yet, at least with regard to what concerns the first twelve centuries, it is here and there not as well-founded as I might wish. However, this is quite understandable, because several things have become clearer since his writing...

---

(*) I have since obtained **Alanus’s** <note>Alain de Lille, a 12th-century theologian.</note> works; but they do not say much toward the clarification of this history.

<meta>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing the thought of how the church...</meta>...diligence preserved the pure Doctrine and Discipline, despite so many *revolutions of affairs outside of her*; how she found herself more openly advocated by CLAUDIUS CLEMENS <note>also known as Claude of Turin, a 9th-century bishop known for his opposition to image worship</note>, her Overseer, in the Ninth Century; and how she, subsequently expanding herself into *Italy*, *Germany*, *Flanders*, and deeper into *France*, was emphatically strengthened and built up through the service of BERENGARIUS, PETRUS DE BRUIS, HENRY OF TOULOUSE, ARNAUD <note>likely Arnold of Brescia</note>, PETER WALDO, and others: while *Rome*, for its part, convened church council after church council against her, and in all sorts of ways slandered, hated, reviled, banished, cursed, and drove her out, even killing multitudes of her members. All this brings me to the end of the Twelfth Century, or the year of our Lord 1200.

Here it seemed to me I could make a suitable division, to begin another work or volume with the introduction of the *Inquisition* and *Crusades* against these Believers, and to end with the dawn of the Reformation, under the concept of the Middle History of these Professors <note>original: "Belyders," meaning those who openly profess their faith</note>. Meanwhile, the Sixteenth, Seventeenth, and that part of the Eighteenth Century that has passed until now, in the form of the Latest History of the WALDENSIANS, can provide the material for a third volume.

Thus there still remains a great road for us to travel: yet, we are encouraged, under Divine assistance and blessing, to proceed upon it. And it will grieve us all the less if we may hear that this work of ours is not disapproved of by modest and steady readers. It will also help me greatly if I may see that scholars and historians are willing to offer me a hand in sending such reports as they believe [may serve me].

# PREFACE.

...could have known, just as in probably sixty years (for that is how long it has been since he published his work <note>The author is referring to Jean Léger, whose definitive history of the Waldensians was published in 1669, roughly 63 years before this preface was written.</note>), others will know things better than we are currently able to observe them.

*As for my way of writing, I have endeavored to write understandably and without offense; and I have applied myself, as much as I was able, to observe a regular spelling based on reason. My style will at times be somewhat slower, then somewhat more lively; especially when the misdeeds of Rome, and the innocent-falsely-hereticized <note>The author uses a compound Dutch word "onnoozel-verketterde" to describe people who were guiltless but branded as heretics by the Church.</note>, hunted, and suffering innocence, stirred me. This the Roman Papists <note>original: "Roomschpauffeiyken" — a period-specific Dutch term for Catholics</note>, or their supporters (should they at any time read this writing of mine), must take in good part. I am a Protestant, and an advocate for my Church; I would therefore have had to wrong my cause, if I had wanted to limit myself to writing those things indifferently and in cold blood.*

*Nevertheless, they must do me the justice of acknowledging that I have only spoken out against faults and injustices; otherwise, it would deeply grieve my heart, as I can testify through God's Grace that, just as I love all Christians and sincerely wish to seek their temporal and eternal salvation at all hours, so also the blindness of those prone to persecution <note>The author refers to those with a "Vervolgzugt" or a thirst for persecution.</note> pains my soul. May the Great and All-Good Merciful One have mercy on them; so that they may see in what urgent peril of soul they are!*

Meanwhile, may God preserve Protestantism by the grace received, and cause it to live worthily according to the same! May He expand it from day to day; and grant it more and more to know and acknowledge the pure truth as it is in JESUS; so that it may be and remain: **THE LORD'S PRAISE ON EARTH!**

->Amsterdam, the 14th of November 1732.<-

### OF THE

## WALDENSIANS.

<note>original: "Historie der Waldensen." The Waldensians (or Vaudois) are a Christian movement that originated in the late 12th century. Often persecuted as heretics in the Middle Ages, they are viewed by the author of this work as precursors to the Protestant Reformation due to their focus on Biblical authority and apostolic poverty.</note>

### FIRST BOOK.

<margin>
As it was with Israel, so it was with Christ’s Church.

It has happened with the Christian Church almost as it did in former times with God’s Ancient People <note>Referring to the Israelites of the Old Testament.</note>. Great was the kindness of Israel’s youth, the love of her betrothal. As long as that People followed the Lord in the wilderness, in an unsown land, they were themselves a holiness unto the LORD; there was no foreign god among them; Jehovah’s statutes and laws were constantly before the eyes of the children of Jacob (1). But very soon, even while still in the wilderness, and especially after this people had obtained the rest and abundance of Canaan, Jeshurun <note>A poetic or symbolic name for Israel, derived from a Hebrew root meaning "upright."</note> turned—

(1) *Jeremiah* 2:2, 3. *Psalm* 81:10. and 99:7.

<margin>In the Fifteenth Century. A.D. 1416.</margin>
How *Jan Hus*, and *Jerome of Prague*, even at the cost of their lives, stood for the Lord's honor and truth in the *Fifteenth Century*, we now pass by. Italy is separated from France and Germany by that mighty multitude of sky-high mountains, known by the name of *Alps*, which stretch from Savona—or as others prefer, from Oneglia, cities in the territory of Genoa where the Apennine Mountains end—and thus from the Ligurian or Genoese Sea, along France and Germany, to near the Venetian Gulf (1). <margin>Things these Valleys have in common.</margin>
Thus we have given a brief overview of each Valley of the **WALDENSES** in particular. Regarding all of them in common, it is true that their lowest parts are fertile, producing wines and all kinds of other fruits; in this way, they somewhat resemble the soil of the pleasant and fertile Piedmont. That region, watered by more than thirty rivers, both large and small, might be called another Egypt, if only the Lord’s Israel <note>A metaphorical reference to the Waldensian people, comparing their plight to that of the biblical Israelites</note> had the freedom to live in its Goshen <note>original: "Gosen"; a fertile region in ancient Egypt where the Israelites resided, here used to represent a place of safety and abundance</note>—I mean the Valleys. <margin>State of the VALLEY CHURCHES at the beginning of the Ninth Century, A.D. 801.</margin>
At the beginning of the ninth century, we see more clearly how things stood with the CHURCHES of the VALLEYS. <meta>This page continues the philological argument from page 179, moving from the internal evidence of the poem "The Noble Lesson" to a broader explanation of the etymology of the name "Waldensian." The author argues that the name is geographical rather than derived from Peter Waldo.</meta>

### History of the Waldensians.

...truth strengthened. He must be a man of singular merit, and of a very <note>This sentence fragment concludes a description of the author of "The Noble Lesson" from the previous page.</note>

of which we speak in the Text, and which flourished in the middle of the *Eleventh Century* <note>The 1000s.</note>, the honored Reader will easily perceive, when he considers that the name of WALDENSIANS, through a slight change, comes from the Valleys, which in Latin <note>original: "Valles"</note> are called *Valleys*, and in the language of the VALLEYS <note>Referring to the Occitan or Piedmontese dialect used by the inhabitants.</note>, (a mixture of Italian and French, and thus a corrupted Latin,) are called *Valli* and *Vaux*; from which the Inhabitants of the same are named *Valdesi* and *Vaudesi*; which, by the Historians who have since written in Latin, became *Vallenses* and *Valdenses*, and with us has become *Waldensians*. Consequently, the name has no other meaning than *Valley-dwellers* or *Inhabitants of the Valleys*. 

This was the name given specifically to the Inhabitants of the valleys of the Alps for many Centuries, without any reference to Religion or opinion; but when these Christians placed themselves more openly against Rome, they were given a name after their first and constant dwelling places—the VALLEYS—from which all the other branches sprang. This was done to identify them because they had no particular leader <note>The author is refuting the Catholic claim that the group was a "sect" founded by Peter Waldo in the 12th century.</note>, but only desired to be called *Christians* or *Followers of the Apostles*. In the same manner, the name of *Bohemians*, *Augsburgers*, and the like has been given to all those who embraced the faith first taught and established in those places. Similarly, they were called *Albigensians* after the city of Albi, *Picards* after Picardy, and *Montignards*, or Mountaineers, after their Mountains. He who is so inclined may see what Leger <note>Jean Léger (1615–1670), a pastor and author of a famous history of the Waldensians.</note> brings forward in *History of the Vaudois, Vol. I. p. 16, 17.* (drawn from *Beza's Illustrious Men, p. 985* <note>Theodore Beza (1519–1605), a major Protestant reformer and successor to Calvin.</note> and from *Coignard's Treatise of Pauzin Joanna, p. 8*).

The author asserts that the group is named for its geographic origin in the Alps rather than a human founder, comparing the name to other regional religious labels like Albigensians or Bohemians.</summary>

### SIXTH BOOK.

<margin>Condition of the WALDENSIANS at the beginning of the Twelfth Century.</margin>
The more progress the WALDENSIANS made, the greater the hatred of the Apostates <note>In this context, "Apostates" refers to the established Roman Church, which the author views as having fallen away from the original purity of the Gospel</note> grew against them. With the beginning of the Twelfth Century, the time seemed to have come when anyone who could kill them believed they were doing God a service. Their Doctrine—however Evangelical <note>The term "Evangelical" here refers to a strict adherence to the teachings of the four Gospels</note> it might be, and only seeking to banish the idol of human inventions <note>A common Reformation-era term for religious traditions and rituals not explicitly commanded in the Bible</note> from the Lord’s Temple—was something so abominable in the eyes of the corrupt Church that it did not spare even the most innocent life. What am I saying? Even an irreproachable walk of life was frequently taken as a sign of WALDENSIANISM <note>Original: "Waldensery." This term was often used by persecutors to label any pious or sober behavior as evidence of heresy</note>, and for that reason alone, it was immediately doomed to death. "HE IS A WALDENSIAN,"

### History of the Waldensians.

<margin>A.D. 1119.</margin>
Pope **Calixtus** II saw a Council <note>The Council of Toulouse held in 1119.</note> established. The Pope, then in France, was present there; the assembly consisted of several Cardinals, as well as Archbishops and Bishops of Guienne (2). Among ten rules that were made at this Church Council, the third asserted: "that the so-called heretics (by which was meant **Peter of Bruys** <note>Petrus de Bruis, an influential preacher who challenged the Catholic hierarchy and sacramental system.</note> and his followers), who rejected the Lord's Supper, Infant Baptism, Marriage, and the other sacraments, should be driven out of the Church and suppressed by the Secular Power <note>Civil or governmental authorities used to enforce church decrees.</note>"; that is to say: those who contradicted Transubstantiation <note>The doctrine that the bread and wine in the Eucharist become the actual substance of Christ's body and blood.</note>; who did not hold Marriage to be a sacrament <note>The reformers viewed it as a civil or social contract rather than a ritual conferring divine grace.</note>; and who judged Infant Baptism not necessary for salvation, but instead judged that this Seal of the Covenant <note>A term for baptism as a sign of God's promise.</note> was best postponed until years of discernment and understanding (3). After the Teacher has instructed his Pupil *what he is, namely a rational and mortal creature; and that God created him to know Him, to serve Him, and to be saved through His grace*; he then gives him an idea from *1 Corinthians XIII. verse 9* <note>While the text cites verse 9, the virtues of faith, hope, and love are famously listed in 1 Corinthians 13:13.</note> regarding what his salvation (that is, the necessary requirement on his part for salvation) consists of, namely in *Faith, Hope, and Love*. He explains Faith using *Hebrews XI. verse 1*, showing that true Faith is not dead, but active in Love; and that a dead faith indeed believes that there is a God, but does not believe *in* God. 

Following this, he leads his Pupil to the *Twelve Articles of the Universal Christian Faith* <note>Commonly known as the Apostles' Creed.</note>, and asks him: *from what can he know that he believes in God?* The Pupil answers: *from the keeping of God's Commandments*, and having the summary of them before his eyes; namely the *Love of God and Neighbor*: showing that *Jesus is the Foundation, without whom one cannot do this in a way pleasing to God*. Then he treats Faith in the Son, and in the Holy Spirit; of the Mystery of the *Holy Trinity*, of the

true *Service* and *Worship of God*, rejecting the service of images <note>original: *Beeldendienst*; the practice of venerating icons or statues, which the Waldensians viewed as idolatry.</note> etc.; and of *Prayer*. These things were obtained through Living Faith and true Repentance, by the favor and gift of God, according to His promises. And after having refuted the Antichristian errors against this Grace, he concludes by giving a concept of the *Communion of Saints* and the obtaining of *Eternal Life*. A branch of the river Rhône, which separates from that river just above Arles and forms the island of Camargue (where *Gaius Marius* <note>A famous Roman general and statesman (c. 157–86 BC)</note> is said to have once been encamped), runs half an hour to the east past Saint-Gilles, and discharges two hours from there into the Mediterranean Sea (1). Pagan idolatry had, so it is said, still left its traces there in certain old ruins of a Temple and a Rostrum <note>original: 'Leerſtoels', referring to a place of teaching or a pulpit</note>, which were found in that small town and its neighborhood (2); but no less had the bloodlust and spirit of persecution of the ancient pagans remained there. The Rhône, upon whose flow the city was founded and which empties into the Mediterranean Sea sixty hours <note>Distances were often measured in "hours," referring to the time it took to travel the distance by boat or on foot.</note> further downstream, receives into itself just a little below the city the Saône, which flows through the middle of the town. Thus, being situated on two famous and far-reaching rivers, it could receive and send its merchandise from and to all places. <margin>The Clergy attacks him.</margin>
This struck the carnal Clergy too closely. It was not to be tolerated, they thought, that a layman—and one, so they believed, who was not ordained, or at least did not derive his authority for that work from Rome—should instruct and preach to the people. Furthermore, to have to hear that they were misleading the people, obscuring the truth, and were utterly corrupt; to have to see that their fat incomes ran the risk of becoming lean—that was intolerable. Therefore, they sent an order and command to **WALDO** that he must cease preaching and teaching at his house and come to Church, or else they would see what should be done with him; should he be disobedient, he could fear the <term>Ban|Excommunication, an official decree excluding someone from the religious community.</term> (1). But he, being too well instructed that where God commands one must never remain silent, even if it should cost honor and property, body and life, gave them as answer: "that everyone was bound [to obey] the Word of the Lord; *Search the Scriptures*, and *Flee from Idolatry*..."

*Alexander* arrived in France in the year 1163, where he was welcomed and received with the utmost respect by both the King of France and the King of England. Having celebrated the Easter feast in Paris, he traveled to Tours, located 50 hours from that city and 90 from Lyons. Here he convened a Council for the 28th of May: his primary objective was to establish his authority in France against that of *Victor* III, his <term>rival|An 'anti-pope' supported by the Holy Roman Emperor, creating a schism where two men claimed to be the rightful Pope.</term>, who was supported by the Emperor. When the appointed time arrived, there appeared in the Church of St. Maurice 17 Cardinals, 124 Bishops, 414 Abbots, and a multitude of other persons (1). Among this procession were, as we suspect, also the enemies of WALDO; who seem to have seized this opportunity to completely blacken the reputation of him and his followers, and on this occasion, through Papal authority, to give free rein to their rage against the Right-believing <note>The author uses 'Right-believing' (Dutch: *Regtgeloovigen*) to refer to the Waldensians, signaling his sympathy for their cause as proto-Protestants.</note> [Waldensians] to...

They are said to have answered in the negative, stating instead that they adhered to the writings of the New Testament.

-># History of the Waldenses.<-

<margin>Aragon. 1194 AD.</margin>This was openly seen in Aragon, where the WALDENSES, as in other parts of Spain, had also spread (2). *Alfonso*, King of Aragon, accompanied by the Bishops of his Kingdom, published a very cruel Edict <note>The Dutch "Plakaet" refers to an official public ordinance or decree</note> against them in the year 1194, by which they, as enemies of the cross of Christ and violators of his Religion, were driven out of the land and exposed to all kinds of foul and cruel treatment (3).

The *Thirteenth* and following centuries contain no fewer disasters, but an even fiercer rage against these Sincere Followers of JESUS: as we see them being put to death by the thousands in all sorts of cruel ways; in which we see the unholy *Inquisition* <term>Inquisition|A powerful judicial system established by the Papacy to detect and suppress heresy</term> established against them, the all-devastating *Crusades* <term>Crusades|While usually referring to wars in the Holy Land, here it refers to the Albigensian Crusade and subsequent military actions against European "heretics"</term> turned against them, and consider them everywhere hunted, inhumanly tortured, and horribly murdered. Whose heart does not shrink at the sight of such cruelty against the innocent? Whose soul does not languish at the sight of so many streams of blood, leaking from the hearts of our blessed and dearly beloved predecessors? ->### History of the Waldensians.<-

382

...to leave [this] to another pen, and to close these pages with a brief word.

<margin>CONCLUSION of this century, and of this short Scene <note>original: "Tafreel," meaning a scene, picture, or tableau</note> of Ancient Waldensian History.</margin>

You see, Christians! who with me have obtained an equally precious faith through the mercy of our God, the Lord’s People at the end of this Century being attacked from all sides, slandered, hated, cursed, driven away; you see the Lord’s *Dove* barely finding any rest for the sole of her foot. <note>This is a biblical allusion to Noah’s dove in Genesis 8:9, symbolizing the Waldensians as a peaceful people finding no place of safety from the "flood" of persecution.</note> Can we imagine all that fear, all that anxiety, all that sorrow, pain, and misery, all those tears, poverty, struggles, and sufferings of these Christians? Then let us think of the invaluable happiness that we enjoy in this thrice-blessed Netherlands; living safely in Christian freedom. What gratitude must we not incessantly bring to You, O all-good GOD! for that which is priceless! Oh, what happiness! Here, peace-loving Shepherds <note>A metaphor for the clergy or ministers of the church</note>, under the governance of the most modest Authorities, will never force those who have strayed, but beseech them; never drive them away, but seek them out; never slaughter and eat them, but heal them and graze them in pure clover. Here one builds upon that foundation: THE CONSCIENCE FREE. That source of all blessing, that unshakable foundation of the

...most flourishing State; that fruitful Mother of Love, Heavenly Wisdom, and Concord; that so human, so Christian, so divine Principle—may it inspire, in imitation of our so praiseworthy Authorities, every subject, and make him practice Truth in Love, and Love in Truth! Thus I see (if I may be permitted to use David’s words here) <note>This refers to the biblical King David, traditionally considered the author of the Book of Psalms. The following italicized passage is a paraphrase of Psalm 85:9–13.</note> *His salvation here always over those who fear Him, so that honor may dwell in our Land; I always see there, Loving-kindness and Truth meeting each other; Righteousness and Peace kissing each other; Truth springing out of the Earth and Righteousness looking down from Heaven: also shall the Lord give that which is good and our Land shall yield its Fruit. Righteousness shall go before His face, and He shall set them in the way of His footsteps.* SO BE IT NOW AND ALWAYS!
